claims.claim: Memory is a product of brain plasticity, which involves structural changes within synapses that create associations between stimuli.
claims.excerpt: Memory, the cognitive process of storing and retrieving past experiences, learning and recognition, is a product of brain plasticity, the structural changes within synapses that create associations between stimuli.
claims.context: Brain plasticity refers to structural changes within synapses that create associations between stimuli to form memories.

claims.claim: Memory processes are stabilized and enhanced by nocturnal sleep and daytime naps.
claims.excerpt: Memory processes have been shown to be stabilized and enhanced (sped up and/or integrated) and memories better consolidated by nocturnal sleep and daytime naps.
claims.context: Nocturnal sleep and daytime naps contribute to the stabilization, enhancement, and consolidation of memories.

claims.claim: Declarative memories are believed to be enhanced by slow-wave sleep.
claims.excerpt: Generally, declarative memories are believed to be enhanced by slow-wave sleep, while non-declarative memories are enhanced by rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, although there are some inconsistencies among experimental results.
claims.context: Slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep are linked to different types of memory enhancement.

claims.claim: Most studies point to specific deficits in declarative memories that form pre or post REM sleep deprivation.
claims.excerpt: Most studies point to the specific deficits in declarative memories that form pre or post REM sleep deprivation.
claims.context: Studies examine how REM sleep deprivation affects declarative memories.

claims.claim: Deficits in non-declarative memory occur pre or post NREM sleep deprivation.
claims.excerpt: Conversely, deficits in non-declarative memory occur pre or post NREM sleep deprivation.
claims.context: NREM sleep deprivation is associated with deficits in non-declarative memory.

claims.claim: A proposed dual-step memory hypothesis suggests that optimal learning occurs when the memory trace is initially processed in SWS and then REM sleep.
claims.excerpt: There is also a proposed dual-step memory hypothesis suggesting that optimal learning occurs when the memory trace is initially processed in SWS and then REM sleep.
claims.context: The dual-step memory hypothesis suggests a sequence of slow-wave sleep followed by REM sleep for optimal learning.

claims.claim: Firing sequences in hippocampal ensembles during spatial learning are also active during sleep.
claims.excerpt: A study by Peigneux et al., (2004) noted that the firing sequences in the hippocampal ensembles during spatial learning are also active during sleep, which shows that post training sleep has a role in processing spatial memories.
claims.context: Peigneux et al. conducted a study in 2004 examining hippocampal ensemble activity during sleep after spatial learning.

claims.claim: Hippocampal activity during slow-wave sleep positively correlates with the improvement on the virtual tour task the following day.
claims.excerpt: The finding noted that the amount of hippocampal activation during slow-wave sleep positively correlated to the improvement on the virtual tour task the following day, which indicates that hippocampal activity during sleep correlates with the improvement in memory performance.
claims.context: Researchers used PET scans and fMRI to monitor cerebral blood flow as a marker of synaptic activity during a virtual tour task.

claims.claim: Modulation of the hippocampus leads to plastic changes in the brain and ultimately an improvement in performance.
claims.excerpt: This modulation of the hippocampus leads to plastic changes in the brain and ultimately an improvement in performance.
claims.context: Learning-dependent modulation in hippocampal activity while sleeping processes previously learned episodic and spatial memory traces.

claims.claim: Acetylcholine is an excitatory neurotransmitter that increases to near waking levels during REM sleep compared to lower levels during slow-wave sleep.
claims.excerpt: Acetylcholine is an excitatory neurotransmitter that is seen to increase to near waking levels during REM sleep while compared to lower levels during slow-wave sleep.
claims.context: Acetylcholine levels fluctuate across different sleep stages, comparing REM sleep to slow-wave sleep.

claims.claim: High levels of acetylcholine promote information attained during wakefulness to be stored in the hippocampus.
claims.excerpt: High levels of ACh would promote information attained during wakefulness to be stored in the hippocampus.
claims.context: Acetylcholine affects the functioning of the hippocampus-dependent memory system.
